Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp. Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Jenkins, Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp.'s Q3 2023 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Tom Reilly, Chief Financial Officer; and Mike Thornton, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp. delivered solid results in Q3, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust production growth averaging 80,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, with meaningful capital efficiencies capturing over $45 million in savings year-to-date. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on environmental stewardship, marking our safest year on record with spill volumes down 52% and proactive remediation ahead of schedule. We are focused on advancing our refining operations, where high utilization and resilient margins contributed significantly to the quarter's success. Finally, we are taking steps to optimize future capital deployment, guiding to disciplined spending that supports 12-15% production growth into 2024 while targeting superior returns.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Tom Reilly to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Tom Reilly: Thank you, Johnathan. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.5 billion, up 15% year-over-year. Operating income was $600 million, and net income was $450 million. We generated $800 million in free cash flow and returned $300 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $4 billion in debt and $1.5 billion in cash.

Before moving to operations, let me provide a detailed walkthrough of our capital expenditure performance, focusing on the drilling, completion, and facilities breakdown—budget versus actual. We'll reference Slide 12 in the investor deck for the visuals.

First, a high-level overview: For full-year 2023, we guided to total upstream CapEx of $1.2 billion, allocated roughly 45% to drilling, 45% to completions, and 10% to facilities. This reflects our disciplined focus on high-margin drilling and completions in the Permian Delaware Basin, where we hold over 150,000 net acres of Tier 1 inventory with breakevens below $35 WTI. Q3 spend came in at $285 million, putting us at 72% of budget through nine months, on track for full-year execution at or below $1.18 billion. We've captured $45 million in CapEx savings year-to-date, driven by service cost deflation and operational efficiencies, offsetting some inflationary pressures in steel and tubulars.

Drilling has been our strongest performer, with year-to-date spend at $485 million against a $540 million budget—a 10% underrun equating to about $55 million saved, primarily from rig productivity gains and a favorable service pricing environment. Our average Permian rig count held steady at 7 rigs—5 in the Delaware Basin targeting the Wolfcamp A and B benches, and 2 in the Midland for Second White interval development. We've drilled 52 horizontal wells year-to-date, averaging 12,500-foot laterals, up 15% from last year.

Key drivers include optimized pad drilling sequences, drilling 4-6 wells per pad in our Southern Delaware assets, reducing mobilization costs by 12% per well. Partnering with SLB and Halliburton on advanced rotary steerable systems and high-torque top drives allowed us to cut average days per 10,000 feet from 2.8 to 2.4—mirroring efficiencies seen at peers like Pioneer and Continental Resources. Regionally, Delaware Basin day rates softened to $22,000 from $25,000 budgeted, thanks to ample rig availability amid OPEC+ cuts stabilizing WTI around $80. We did see a slight overrun in the Eagle Ford, where Q3 weather delays added $3 million, but that's more than offset by Permian outperformance.

Strategically, these savings are being redeployed to accelerate inventory turns, with drilling lead times now under 90 days for new pads. Breakevens on new Delaware wells are down to $32 per barrel, positioning us well against hedging at $75-80 for 60% of 2024 production.

Completions came in at $515 million year-to-date versus $540 million planned—a solid 5% underrun, or $25 million saved. We've completed 48 wells, focusing on simultaneous fracs across 3-4 wells per pad to minimize deferrals. Average frac stages per well hit 55, with proppant loadings at 2,500 lbs/ft using our proprietary ApexBlend—80/100 mesh sand sourced locally from our Silo Creek mine to cut logistics costs by 8%.

Technical initiatives include implementing dissolvable frac balls and engineered diverters from Liberty Energy, reducing stage times by 20%, from 8 to 6.4 hours per stage. This echoes ExxonMobil's Guyana playbook but tailored for Permian stack pay. Cost per stage averaged $45,000, down 7% year-over-year despite sand inflation—now stabilizing post-Ukraine supply chain disruptions. In the Bakken, where we have a smaller footprint, completions ran 3% over budget due to higher water sourcing costs amid drought conditions, but Permian efficiencies absorbed that.

Regionally, Delaware remains dominant: 80% of our frac crews are there, benefiting from the basin's infrastructure maturity. We're on pace for 180 gross completions full-year, with IP30 rates averaging 1,800 Boe/d—top-quartile versus Permian peers per Enverus analytics.

Facilities represent our modest overrun at $132 million versus $120 million budgeted—about $12 million above plan. This category supports midstream tie-ins, artificial lift installations, and water management infrastructure critical for scaling production.

Breakout includes $60 million on gas gathering and compression upgrades in Delaware to handle richer BTU gas at 1,300 BTU/scf, tying into Matterhorn Express Pipeline capacity we secured last year. $40 million on saltwater disposal facilities, including our new 40,000 bbl/d injection well in Reeves County, compliant with Texas Railroad Commission regs. The overrun stems from 15% steel price escalation prompted by U.S. Steel tariffs and EPC contractor delays on two subsea tie-backs in the Gulf of Mexico, where we're developing our Lucius extension with partial JV interest alongside Shell.

Mitigations include value engineering: switching to fiberglass tanks from steel where possible, saving $2 million, and leveraging drone inspections to defer $1.5 million in maintenance CapEx. Long-term, this builds resilience—our facilities now support 20% production growth without proportional spend increases.

Net, we're $22 million under budget year-to-date across drilling and completions, partially offset by facilities, for a $10 million total underrun. Margins expanded to 28% on D&C costs, driven by 10-15% efficiencies in lateral lengths and cluster spacing optimized via our ApexAI petrophysics model—machine learning on core data from 500+ offsets.

Looking forward, Q4 CapEx guidance is $300-320 million, full-year landing at $1.15-1.18 billion. We'll flex up drilling if WTI holds above $75, targeting 65-70 gross wells. Risks include service inflation if rig counts rebound, but our multi-year contracts with Patterson-UTI lock in 85% of rates. This positions Apex for 12-15% production growth to 85,000 Boe/d in 2024, with ROCE exceeding 25%.

Turning now to our refining segment, where we delivered solid results amid a volatile macro environment. Apex operates a world-class portfolio of seven refineries with a total atmospheric crude distillation capacity of 2.1 million barrels per day, spanning the US Gulf Coast, Midwest PADD 2, Northwest Europe, and our joint venture in Singapore. Our Nelson Complexity Index averages 11.2 across the slate, positioning us well for high-value product yields. Let me break this down into throughput, margins, and operational efficiency.

Starting with throughput, we processed 1.92 million barrels per day in Q3, reflecting a robust 91% capacity utilization rate—up 400 basis points sequentially from Q2's 87% and flat year-over-year. This marks our strongest quarterly volume since Q4 2019 pre-pandemic levels. Key drivers included robust gasoline and diesel demand recovery in the US, where summer driving season pushed distillate runs higher, and steady jet fuel uptake in Europe as air travel rebounded to 85% of 2019 levels per IATA data.

Regionally, our USGC assets—Limpet Bay and Echo Point refineries—led the way at 1.1 million bpd, achieving 94% utilization despite minor weather disruptions from Tropical Storm Barry, which shaved just 2 days of runs. We opportunistically ran heavier Canadian WCS and Latin American Maya crudes, blending 35% discounted heavy sour grades into our slate, which helped optimize costs. In PADD 2, our Joliet complex hit 98% utilization on ULSD mandates and Midwest export logistics. Europe saw 650,000 bpd at 89% utilization, buoyed by Ural crude discounts amid Russian sanctions, while our Singapore JV contributed 170,000 bpd equity share, capitalizing on Asian middle distillate cracks.

Looking ahead, we expect Q4 throughput to average 92-94% utilization, supported by seasonal distillate strength, though we're monitoring potential USGC hurricane risks via our enhanced weather modeling.

Refining margins remained healthy at an average realized crack spread of $14.50 per barrel on a 3-2-1 basis—down 18% sequentially from Q2's $17.70 but up 12% year-over-year. This compares favorably to the USGC benchmark 3-2-1, which averaged $13.80, and the Northwest Europe 3-1-2 at €11.50 per barrel equivalent. Product slate performance was mixed: gasoline cracks held firm at $22/bbl WTI (Group 3 basis) on ethanol blending economics and California CARB demand, while ULSD margins expanded to $18/bbl on transatlantic arbitrage flows. Jet cracks softened to $15/bbl amid inventory builds, but our high jet yield—12% at Limpet Bay—mitigated impacts.

Secondary margins were a bright spot, with our alkylation and hydrocracking units driving $4.20 per barrel in incremental value through superior octane and cetane production. We captured $250 million in co-product credits from petchem intermediates like benzene and propylene, up 15% YoY, leveraging ties to our upstream petrochemical integration. Heavy crude discounts—WCS at $18/bbl under WTI—added $1.10/bbl to net realizations, though Brent-WTI backwardation pressured light sweet economics.

Strategically, we're hedging 60% of Q4 cracks via futures and swaps to lock in $13+ floors, while our proprietary crack forecasting model, refined with AI-driven Brent-WTI dynamics, positions us to pivot slates dynamically.

Operational efficiency hit new highs this quarter, with total refining costs per barrel at $5.80—down 7% YoY and 4% sequentially, beating our internal target of $6.00. Variable costs declined to $3.20/bbl on optimized crude blending and lower natural gas prices ($2.40/MMBtu Henry Hub average), while fixed maintenance spend came in at $180 million, 10% under budget post our phased turnaround program.

Turnaround performance was exemplary: We completed statutory work at Echo Point and Joliet with zero safety incidents and 15% faster completion times via modular pre-fab techniques, minimizing downtime to just 22 days aggregate. Uptime exceeded 98.5%, our best in five years. Yield optimization initiatives shone through—middle distillate yields rose 1.8 percentage points to 48.5% via hydrocracker debottlenecks at Limpet Bay, adding $120 million in value. Energy intensity improved 5% to 85,000 BTU per barrel, on track for our 2030 Scope 1+2 reduction goal, driven by electrification pilots and hydrogen blending in fired heaters.

Technically, we're advancing our $450 million CapEx program: Q3 saw first hydrotreater output from our renewable diesel conversion at Joliet, producing 10,000 bpd RBD on used cooking oil feedstock under IRA incentives, with 85% yields and $25/bbl D4R margins. This de-risks our pathway to 20% biofuels by 2027, tapping EU RED III and California LCFS credits. In Singapore, our JV's coker revamp boosted VGO conversion 12%, enhancing flexibility for high-sulfur fuel oil amid IMO 2020 residuals.

Overall, refining contributed $650 million in segment EBITDA, up 8% YoY, with ROIC at 22%—top quartile per Wood Mackenzie benchmarks. We're prioritizing high-complexity, export-oriented assets, divesting a low-NCI Midwest mini-mill by year-end for $300 million proceeds to fund growth CapEx. Amid OPEC+ cuts and China demand softness, our global footprint hedges regional risks, with 40% export volumes to Latin America and Asia.

For the full year, we guide to $14-16/bbl cracks, 90%+ utilization, and costs under $6.00/bbl, positioning refining for $2.4-2.6 billion EBITDA. This underscores our disciplined approach: optimize the slate today, transform for energy transition tomorrow.

One more area I'd like to highlight before handing off is our environmental performance, specifically around spills, incidents, and remediation efforts. Safety and sustainability are non-negotiable pillars of our strategy, especially as we navigate heightened ESG scrutiny from investors like BlackRock and Vanguard, and tightening regulations from the EPA and BOEM. I'm proud to report that 2023 is on track to mark our safest year on record, with meaningful progress across the board.

In the first nine months of 2023, we experienced four reportable spills under EPA Tier 1 and Tier 2 classifications, totaling 900 barrels—predominantly produced water releases from our onshore operations, with just 120 barrels of crude oil. That's already a strong reduction from prior years, and our annualized spill rate stands at 0.12 barrels per million barrels produced, well below the American Petroleum Institute's upstream benchmark of 0.45 for Permian operators and significantly outperforming peers like Occidental in normalized terms.

Regionally, our Permian Basin assets—where we averaged 450,000 bopd—saw zero crude spills, thanks to our aggressive pipeline integrity program. We had two minor produced water releases there, totaling 400 barrels, both contained within secondary containment berms within hours. In the Gulf of Mexico, our flagship Thunder Horse South platform reported one incident: an 80-barrel synthetic-based mud release during drilling ops, classified as Tier 2. Rapid deployment of our spill response vessel, the Apex Responder, and boom deployment limited shoreline impact to under 0.5 miles, with full dispersant application per NETC best practices. Our small North Sea position had one negligible incident under 50 barrels from a legacy well workover, aligning with UK BEIS reporting thresholds.

These trends stem from proactive investments. Our mean time between failures on critical pipelines improved 25% to 1,200 days, driven by enhanced in-line inspection runs using multi-threaded electromagnetic acoustic transducer tools from Baker Hughes. We've also rolled out AI-powered leak detection across 70% of our 5,000-mile gathering system, integrating with SCADA and fiber-optic distributed acoustic sensing. This tech flagged 12 potential anomalies pre-emptively this year, averting an estimated 600 barrels of potential releases.

On remediation, we've spent $11.5 million through nine months on cleanup and restoration—down significantly from prior periods—while resolving 100% of cases ahead of regulatory timelines. For the Gulf incident, we completed bioremediation using proven effective microbes, achieving 95% hydrocarbon degradation in 60 days, followed by independent third-party validation via EPA Method 8015 GC-MS analysis. Onshore, our Permian efforts focused on enhanced groundwater monitoring with passive diffusion samplers, confirming no off-site migration in all cases. We've reclaimed 200 acres of disturbed land to native rangeland specs, boosting our cumulative remediation success rate to 98.7% since 2020.

These outcomes directly support our financial health: lower incident rates shaved millions off insurance premiums and avoided potential fines, even amid WTI's volatility around $75-85 per barrel. We're ahead of the curve on SEC climate disclosure rules, with Scope 1+2 emissions down 18% year-to-date, partly from flaring reductions tied to fewer venting incidents. Looking ahead, we're allocating $50 million in CapEx for 2024 to expand drone-based hyperspectral imaging for real-time spill detection—partnering with SLB's Delfi platform—and targeting a 30% further spill volume cut. This positions us not just for compliance, but for premium valuation multiples in an era where ESG funds are driving 20% of E&P M&A.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Thornton for an operational update.

Mike Thornton: Thank you, Tom. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 80,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought Southern Delaware Pad 15 online, which is expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives, including those highlighted in upstream efficiencies and refining optimizations.

To wrap up my prepared remarks on the future, let me provide some color on our capital expenditure guidance, including future spending plans through 2026 and the expected returns that underpin our disciplined allocation framework. We've maintained a relentless focus on capital efficiency and high-return inventory in this volatile macro environment, with WTI Brent averaging around $78 per barrel in Q3 and Henry Hub gas holding steady near $2.80 per MMBtu.

For full-year 2024, we're guiding to $2.6 billion, up slightly from prior expectations due to accelerated completions in the Permian and favorable service cost deflation. This represents about 55% of our full-year adjusted EBITDAX forecast of $4.7 billion, leaving ample room for our progressive dividend—which we're increasing 10% to $1.40 per share annually—and $1.2 billion in share repurchases under our ongoing $3 billion program.

Looking ahead, we're guiding to $2.8 billion in 2025 and $3.0 billion in 2026. This ramp reflects our confidence in a multi-year inventory of Tier 1 locations delivering superior economics. Importantly, 85% of this spend is earmarked for upstream development, with the balance split between midstream infrastructure and low-carbon initiatives.

Our upstream program is laser-focused on high-grading our portfolio. In the Permian Basin—which accounts for 65% of our D&C CapEx—we're planning 120 operated wells in 2025, up from 105 next year, emphasizing our core Delaware Basin position spanning over 180,000 net acres. We're pushing lateral lengths to 15,000 feet on average, with multi-well pad drilling incorporating our proprietary ApexStim completion design—4,500 pounds of proppant per foot and engineered diverter tech that's boosted our 30-day IP rates by 18% year-over-year to over 1,800 Boe/d per well. These wells are breakeven below $45 WTI half-cycle, with base-case IRRs north of 60% at $70 oil and paybacks under 9 months. We've got 3.5 years of drilled, uncompleted inventory here, de-risked by extensive fiber-optic diagnostics and machine learning-optimized frac designs.

Shifting to the Eagle Ford, we're allocating $400 million annually, targeting our oil window in Karnes and DeWitt counties. Here, we're deploying electric frack fleets in partnership with Halliburton to cut emissions by 40% and variable costs by 15%, yielding IRRs of 35-45% on our 12-stream inventory.

Internationally, the Gulf of Mexico deepwater remains a growth engine, with $500 million committed through 2026 for subsea tie-backs to our Winterfell FPSO. Winterfell Phase 2 will add 20,000 Boe/d gross by mid-2026 at a sub-$30 breakeven, leveraging Chevron's Anchor infrastructure for low-cost access. We've also sanctioned two wildcats offshore Namibia in our Orange Basin block JV with TotalEnergies, backed by 4D seismic and Venus-analog potential—initial drilling slated for Q4 2025 with NPV10s exceeding $1 billion at $70 Brent.

For midstream and infrastructure, $300-400 million annually: In the Permian, $150 million goes to expanding our Whiting Midstream JV stake, adding 100 MMcf/d of gas processing and crude gathering capacity to capture NGL premiums amid record ethane cracks. We've locked in 70% of 2025 volumes via fee-based contracts, shielding FCF from basis volatility.

Low-carbon and tech initiatives ramp to $100-200 million, or 7% of total CapEx by 2026. We're deploying $120 million into CCUS pilots in the Permian, partnering with Occidental on direct air capture hubs tied to our CO2 EOR floods, targeting 2 MMtpa capture by 2027 with 45Q credits enhancing IRRs to 20%+. Digitally, our ApexAI platform—integrating reservoir simulation with real-time IoT data—has reduced dry hole risk by 25%, while electrification of rigs and pumps is shaving LOE by $1.50/Boe.

At a portfolio level, our 2025-2026 program delivers blended IRRs of 28-32% at $65 WTI / $3.50 gas, with 70% of capital generating >25% IRR and average paybacks of 14 months. We've stress-tested this down to $55 oil, still yielding 18% IRR and positive FCF. This discipline stems from our barbell strategy: low-risk infill in Tier 1 basins like Permian (75% of spend) balanced with high-reward explorers like Namibia and Guyana offsets.

Compared to peers, our CapEx intensity is sub-20% of EV, versus the E&P average of 25%, thanks to 12% year-over-year drilling efficiency gains. We're hedging 60% of 2025 oil at $72 collars to protect returns, while our $8 billion liquidity and net debt-to-EBITDAX of 0.8x give us optionality amid OPEC+ cuts and LNG demand surges.

In summary, this CapEx plan drives 5-7% annual production growth to 450,000 Boe/d by 2026, while generating $2.5+ billion in levered FCF at strip prices—50%+ returned to shareholders. We're not chasing volume; we're chasing value in a world of finite Tier 1 rock.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Brian Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Brian Carter: Good morning, team. Can you provide more detail on the CapEx variances in drilling and facilities, and how you're redeploying those savings?

Tom Reilly: Good morning, Brian. Happy to elaborate. As I detailed earlier, the $55 million underrun in drilling came from rig productivity and softer day rates in the Delaware, while facilities' $12 million overrun was steel-driven but mitigated through value engineering. Those net savings are being redeployed into accelerating Permian pads, keeping us on track for top-quartile breakevens and supporting our flex-up optionality in Q4.

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Lisa Patel: Good morning. What are your expectations for refining throughput and margins heading into Q4, given crack volatility?

Tom Reilly: Good morning, Lisa. We're guiding 92-94% utilization in Q4 with $14-16/bbl cracks full-year, hedging 60% for floors above $13. Our global slate hedges regional risks, and renewable diesel ramps at Joliet add high-margin upside under IRA incentives.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Kim with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Kim: Good morning. Could you please provide more color on environmental incidents and how that ties into your 2024 CapEx for sustainability?

Mike Thornton: Good morning, David. Our spill rate is best-in-class at 0.12 bbls per MMbbls produced, with AI leak detection and rapid response driving the reductions. The $50 million 2024 allocation for drone hyperspectral tech and CCUS pilots not only cuts incidents 30% further but boosts IRRs via credits and premium multiples.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the conference back over to Johnathan Hale for closing remarks.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Operator. In summary, we are pleased with our performance in Q3. We remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering value to our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
